1331.title: The Litany of Loreto
1331.hook: a long chant of Mary's titles
1331.tomorrow: Tower of ivory, house of gold
1331.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Litany of Loreto in churches and at home, sometimes after the rosary or at Marian devotions; a leader calls each title and everyone answers, pray for us.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the undoer of knots: a painting in Augsburg, and patient hands working a ribbon loose. Your line was she undoes knots.

Holy Mother of God. Pray for us. Mother most pure. Pray for us. Seat of wisdom. Pray for us. Morning star. Pray for us. One voice calls, the room answers, and the rhythm rolls on, name after name, like waves on a beach. Some parishes sing it on a Saturday evening; some families say it after the rosary, half asleep on the couch. It's called a litany, and this one takes its name from a small hill town in Italy. Today's word: Loreto.
screen: `ONE VOICE CALLS.` → `THE ROOM ANSWERS.` → `NAME AFTER NAME.`

segments.voice: Loreto is a shrine town in Italy. Tradition says it holds the Holy House, the house of Nazareth where Mary lived, and pilgrims come to pray there. This litany was sung at that shrine, and the Church came to call it by the town's name. Its shape is call and response. It opens by turning to God: Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; and to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, with the answer, have mercy on us. Then it turns to Mary, and the answer changes to pray for us. That small switch holds the whole Catholic understanding of Mary's place: mercy is asked of God; Mary is asked to pray. The names come in families. Mother: Mother of Christ, Mother of the Church, Mother most amiable. Virgin: Virgin most prudent, Virgin most faithful. Pictures borrowed from scripture and old poetry: Mirror of justice, Seat of wisdom, Mystical rose, Ark of the covenant, Gate of heaven, Morning star. Help in trouble: Health of the sick, Refuge of sinners, Comforter of the afflicted, Help of Christians. And Queen: of angels, of apostles, of martyrs, of peace. The list keeps growing. Popes have added names over time; Pope Francis added Mother of mercy, Mother of hope, and Solace of migrants. Why so many? Because one name never covers anyone you love. A mother gets called all sorts of things in a single day, depending on what you need from her. The litany does the same, out loud, together.

segments.voice: If you pray, say five names from the litany slowly and answer each yourself: Seat of wisdom, pray for us; Health of the sick, pray for us; Refuge of sinners, pray for us; Comforter of the afflicted, pray for us; Queen of peace, pray for us. Let a face come with each one, someone sick, someone grieving, someone far from home. If you don't pray, say the five names and let each one rest for a breath.
Loreto. A shrine town in Italy, and the name of the litany sung there: Mary's titles, called and answered, pray for us.

1332.title: Tower of ivory, house of gold
1332.hook: poetic titles from scripture and old hymns
1332.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Litany of Loreto, with titles like Tower of Ivory and House of Gold, in parishes and at home, often after the rosary, answering each title with "pray for us."

segments.voice: Yesterday, Loreto: the litany that calls Mary name after name, each one answered with pray for us. Your line was many names.

In everyday English, an ivory tower is usually a put-down. Say someone lives in one, and you mean they're out of touch. But halfway down the Litany of Loreto, the phrase turns up as a name for a mother. Tower of ivory. House of gold. Then ark of the covenant, gate of heaven, morning star. They're pictures, set side by side, the way someone who loves a person keeps reaching past ordinary words for a better one. Where do they come from, and why pray in them?
screen: `AN IVORY TOWER, USUALLY A PUT-DOWN.` → `HERE, A NAME FOR A MOTHER.` → `PICTURES, NOT SENTENCES.`

segments.voice: Start with the tower. It comes out of a love song. In the Canticle of Canticles, the Song of Songs, a lover praises the beloved line by line, and in the Douay-Rheims one line reads: "Thy neck as a tower of ivory." Some Jewish and Christian readers have heard this poem as being about more than two lovers: God and his people, Christ and the Church, God and the soul. Some Christian writers took its lines and gave them to Mary. It's borrowed love poetry. Ivory is rare, pale and smooth; a tower is strong and stands guard. Together they make something lovely and sturdy at once, a beauty that doesn't break. Then the house of gold. In the Book of Kings, Solomon's Temple is covered inside with gold, and in Exodus the ark of the covenant is overlaid with gold, inside and out. In those stories the gold isn't for show. It marks the place where God chose to dwell. Catholics call Mary a house of gold for the same reason: she carried Christ. The house is precious because of who lives in it. Notice what that does: each title points past her, to the one she held. Catholic teaching about Mary has its careful, exact statements; this stretch began with four of them. The litany speaks another language, the one a child uses about a mother: not a definition, but a pile of names that never quite says enough.
screen: `A LINE FROM A LOVE SONG.` · `LOVELY AND STRONG AT ONCE.` · `GOLD MARKS WHERE GOD DWELLS.` · `A CHILD'S LANGUAGE, NOT A DEFINITION.` · then, large: `THY NECK AS A TOWER OF IVORY.`

If you pray, say that one title with its answer, pray for us; if you don't, let the picture be enough.

1333.title: The mother who stood
1333.hook: Mary, who stood at the cross, as comforter of the afflicted
1333.carry: mary comforts because she stood at the cross
1333.howItsDone: Catholics call on Mary as Comforter of the Afflicted in the Litany of Loreto, and parishes and hospital chaplains often bring the title to people who are sick or grieving, alongside visits and practical help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tower of ivory and house of gold: pictures borrowed from a love song and a golden Temple. Your line was poetry for a mother.

A hospital corridor, late at night. Someone has just had bad news, and a friend sits down beside them. The friend doesn't explain anything or fix anything. Fetches a coffee, sits back down, and stays. Further down the Litany of Loreto, after the towers and the gold, the titles change their tone. Health of the sick. Refuge of sinners. Comforter of the afflicted. Help of Christians. The poetry comes down to the ground. Today's word is the one in the middle.
screen: `A FRIEND WHO STAYS.` → `HEALTH OF THE SICK, REFUGE OF SINNERS.` → `COMFORT OF THE AFFLICTED.`

segments.voice: In the litany's Latin it's consolatrix afflictorum: the one who consoles the afflicted, the people weighed down. The reason begins with Mary's own grief. When she brings her baby to the Temple, an old man named Simeon takes him in his arms and then turns to her. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." The comforter in this title is not someone who was spared. Then the cross. John's Gospel names who was there, and it starts with her: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." No speech. No miracle. She stood. Some Catholics find in that one verb a whole way of comforting: you don't leave, even when there's nothing to say. Then Paul adds a third turn. Writing to the church in Corinth, he says God comforts people in all their trouble so that they can comfort others in theirs, with the same comfort they were given. Comfort, for Paul, travels: received, then handed on. That's how Catholics hear this title. Mary, who knew the sword and stood at the cross, passes on the comfort she received, and when they pray comforter of the afflicted, pray for us, they bring her the people who are going under. And the title quietly describes a job. Anyone can take a shift: the friend in the corridor, the neighbor with a casserole, the text that says I'm here and asks nothing back.
screen: `SHE KNEW THE SWORD HERSELF.` · `AT THE CROSS, SHE STOOD.` · `COMFORT RECEIVED, THEN HANDED ON.` · `A JOB ANYONE CAN TAKE A SHIFT IN.` · then, large: `NOW THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who's carrying something heavy right now, an illness, a loss, a worry they keep mentioning, and stay with them for a few breaths, the way the friend stays in the corridor, without planning any advice. If you pray, name them and add the litany's line, comforter of the afflicted, pray for us; if you don't, simply hold them. And if the heavy thing is yours and it feels like too much, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1334.title: Behold thy mother
1334.hook: a title given by Paul VI at the Second Vatican Council, now a memorial on the Monday after Pentecost
1334.carry: behold thy mother: mary mothers every disciple
1334.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church, on the Monday after Pentecost, and the Litany of Loreto includes the invocation "Mother of the Church, pray for us."

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary who stood at the cross, and comfort received and handed on. Your line was Mary comforts because she stood at the cross.
screen: `MARY COMFORTS BECAUSE SHE STOOD AT THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: "Woman, behold thy son." Words from the cross, in John's Gospel. Jesus is dying, and below him stand two people: his mother, and the disciple the Gospel calls the one whom he loved. He speaks to her first, then turns to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." And John adds a line that's easy to read past: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." At the worst hour, a family is made. Catholics hear that sentence reaching much further than one house.
screen: `WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.` → `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.` → `A FAMILY MADE AT THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: You met this title on day three hundred twenty-three; today, its story. Start with the disciple. John's Gospel never names him in that scene. Catholics read that as an open door: the beloved disciple stands for every disciple, so behold thy mother is spoken to each of them. Some Christians read the scene more simply, as a dying son making sure his mother is looked after. Catholics hold that reading too, and hear more in it. Next, the upper room. In the Acts of the Apostles, after Jesus is taken up, his friends pray together, with one mind, with the women and with Mary, the mother of Jesus. Then comes Pentecost, the coming of the Holy Spirit, sometimes called the Church's birthday. So Mary is there at the birth of Jesus, and in the room when the Church is born. Then the title. During the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul the Sixth gave Mary the name Mother of the Church, and the Catechism puts it in one line: Mother of Christ, Mother of the Church. The Council holds two things together. She is a member of the Church, a believer like the rest. And she mothers it. Last, the calendar. Pope Francis made the title a memorial, on the Monday after Pentecost. That turns the Church from an institution into something more like a crowded kitchen table: people who didn't choose each other, handed to one another, with a mother keeping an eye on them all.
screen: `THE DISCIPLE STANDS FOR EVERY DISCIPLE.` · `IN THE ROOM WHEN THE CHURCH IS BORN.` · `A MEMBER, AND A MOTHER.` · `THE MONDAY AFTER PENTECOST.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Picture the Church not as a building but as a table full of people, starting with one parish you know, then widening: people who serve, people who are tired, people who were hurt, people who walked away, people gathering far off where it costs them. 1335.title: Alma Redemptoris Mater
1335.hook: the Marian antiphon of Advent and Christmas
1335.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours close Night Prayer with an antiphon to Mary; in Advent and the Christmas season it is traditionally the Alma Redemptoris Mater, often sung in Latin chant in monasteries and some parishes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mother of the Church: behold thy mother, from the cross to the upper room. Your line was mother of the church.

When the Church's night prayer is finished, there's one more thing before the silence: a short song to Mary, called an antiphon. Which one depends on the time of year, the way a coat does. In Advent, the dark weeks of waiting before Christmas, and on through the Christmas season, it's this one. It opens with three Latin words that climb slowly, like steps: Alma Redemptoris Mater. Loving mother of the Redeemer. Tradition credits it to a monk, Hermann of Reichenau. Over the next few days the night song changes with the seasons, and i'll follow it around the year with you.
screen: `NIGHT PRAYER ENDS WITH A SONG TO MARY.` → `IT CHANGES WITH THE SEASON.` → `ADVENT AND CHRISTMAS: THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Take it a phrase at a time. First, two pictures. It calls Mary the open gate of heaven, and stella maris, star of the sea. On a dark sea, sailors could steer by a star that stayed put while everything else moved. Advent is a season of waiting for light, and the song gives the people waiting a fixed point to steer by. Then the request, and it's honest. In Latin: succurre cadenti, surgere qui curat, populo. Help the people who are falling, who are trying to get up. Not a people who have it together. A people in the middle of falling, still trying to rise. Then the wonder. While nature marveled, natura mirante, she gave birth to her own holy Creator. A mother holding the one who made her. Nature doesn't explain it; nature marvels. That's Christmas, said in a single breath. Last, the song goes back to the start of the story. It remembers her taking that Ave from Gabriel's mouth, the angel's greeting in Luke's Gospel, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Then it ends where a long day often ends, asking for mercy: peccatorum miserere, have mercy on sinners. Gate, star, falling and rising, wonder, mercy. A whole season, folded small enough to sing before bed.
screen: `GATE OF HEAVEN, STAR OF THE SEA.` · `HELP THE ONES FALLING, TRYING TO RISE.` · `NATURE MARVELS.` · `FROM GABRIEL'S MOUTH, AN AVE.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE, THE LORD IS WITH THEE.`

If you pray, let it be your prayer; if not, let it be music in the dark.

1336.title: Ave Regina Caelorum
1336.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours traditionally close Night Prayer in Lent with the Ave Regina Caelorum, said or sung in Latin chant or in English.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alma Redemptoris Mater: the night song of Advent and Christmas. Your line was star of the sea.

Christmas gets packed away, and the song at the end of night prayer changes. The gate and the star step aside. Then come the ashes, and Lent, and the song that stays through it sounds almost like a herald at a palace door: Ave, Regina caelorum. Hail, queen of heaven. Ave, Domina angelorum. Hail, lady of the angels. Lent is purple cloth, fasting, the long walk toward the cross. Why greet a queen in a season like that? The answer starts in a throne room, far back in the Bible.
screen: `CHRISTMAS PACKED AWAY.` → `HAIL, QUEEN OF HEAVEN.` → `A QUEEN, IN LENT?`

segments.voice: In the Book of Kings, King Solomon is on his throne when his mother, Bathsheba, comes in to speak to him. He stands, goes to meet her, bows to her, and has a throne set for her at his right hand. Catholics call Mary queen for that kind of reason: not because she rules in her own right, but because her son is the king. Then the greetings. Ave, hail. Salve, hail again. Gaude, rejoice. Vale, farewell. The song is built almost entirely of greetings, like someone at a doorway who keeps finding another way to say hello. Then the root and the gate: salve, radix, salve, porta. Hail, root; hail, gate; from you a light rose on the world. The root reaches back to Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse." Jesse was David's father. Christians read the new shoot from that old root as a promise of Christ, born into David's family, and see Mary as the one through whom he came. The gate is the door the light came through, and in Lent, waiting for Easter light, the song keeps pointing at it. Last, the farewell: vale, o valde decora, farewell, you who are so beautiful. Then the final request: pray to Christ for us. A goodbye said before sleep, handing the singers on to her son. So a queen in Lent isn't so odd. Lent walks toward the cross, and this song keeps a door open to the light on the other side.

segments.voice: Let today pass once, quickly, like a train watched from a platform, the morning, the middle, the evening, and then, the way the song does, say goodbye to it. If you pray, close with the antiphon's first words, hail, queen of heaven, hail, lady of the angels, and its last request, pray to Christ for us. If you don't, end with one plain farewell to the day.
Ave Regina Caelorum. Hail, queen of the heavens: the night song of Lent, full of greetings, a root and a gate, and a goodbye before sleep.
Your line: hail, queen of heaven. Queen because her son is king. That's one more on the road.

1337.howItsDone: In the Easter season, from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who pray the Angelus at morning, noon and evening say the Regina Caeli in its place, and it also closes Night Prayer through that season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ave Regina Caelorum, the night song of Lent, with its goodbye before sleep. Your line was hail, queen of heaven.

Noon, and somewhere a church bell rings. For much of the year, the prayer that goes with that bell is the Angelus, which you met on day one hundred three: an angel, a young woman, a yes, and the Word made flesh. But from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who keep the noon bell set the Angelus aside and pray something else. The story has jumped to its ending, and the prayer jumps with it. It's short, and every line ends in the same word, like a door that keeps swinging open: alleluia. Today's word is the Easter prayer to Mary, Regina Caeli.
screen: `NOON, AND A BELL.` → `THE ANGELUS TELLS THE BEGINNING.` → `IN EASTER, THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: In plain English: queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For he whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia, has risen, as he said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia. Start with the first command: rejoice, in Latin laetare. Think back this week to the woman who stood at the cross, whose soul Simeon said a sword would pierce. In the Easter prayer, the first thing said to her is be glad. The one who knew the worst of Friday is told about Sunday. Then the two Latin words in the middle that carry the weight: sicut dixit, as he said. They echo the angel at the empty tomb in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." The prayer doesn't only announce that he rose. It says he kept his word. A promise made before the cross turns out true on the other side of it. Then the alleluias. Through Lent, the Latin Church sets the word alleluia aside; it isn't sung at Mass. At Easter it comes back, and this little prayer can't stop saying it. Last, it still asks: pray for us to God. Even at the height of joy, it turns to Mary for help, the way this whole week has. So in Easter the noon bell rings for a mother told to rejoice because her son kept his promise.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise someone made to you and kept, a friend who showed up, a call returned, and remember the moment you knew they'd kept it; then let it widen: as he said. If you pray, say the Regina Caeli slowly now, with an alleluia at the end of each line. If you don't, hold that kept promise in mind and let it be good news.

Regina Caeli. Queen of heaven: the Easter prayer, rejoice, he is risen. This week's road: many names, poetry for a mother, comfort of the afflicted, mother of the church, star of the sea, hail, queen of heaven, and now rejoice.
